subject: pathology
title: Virchow Triad, Thrombus Architecture, and Inherited Thrombophilia

steps.tx: Pathological intravascular formation of a solid blood clot within uninjured vessels or inappropriate occlusion of an injured vascular lumen is governed by three primary abnormalities. Formulated in nineteenth-century pathology, the **Virchow triad** comprises endothelial injury, alterations in normal blood laminar flow, and hypercoagulability.
steps.say: Virchow triad identifies endothelial injury, abnormal blood flow, and hypercoagulability as causes of thrombosis.

vis.alt: The classical Virchow triad of thrombosis pathophysiology
vis.caption: The classical Virchow triad predisposing to deep venous thrombosis and thromboembolism.

steps.tx: Microscopic evaluation of thrombi formed within flowing arterial or cardiac lumens demonstrates characteristic alternating pale and dark laminations. These microscopic structures represent **lines of Zahn**, composed of pale layers of platelets and fibrin alternating with darker, erythrocyte-rich layers, confirming ante-mortem intravascular formation.
steps.say: Lines of Zahn are alternating pale platelet-fibrin and dark erythrocyte laminations formed in flowing blood.

nodes.label: Rapid Blood Flow Deposits Platelets and Entangled Fibrin
Intermittent Blood Flow Stasis Traps Packed Erythrocytes
Alternating Laminations Form Classic Microscopic Lines of Zahn

steps.tx: Distinguishing an ante-mortem thrombus from post-mortem blood clotting is critical at autopsy. Unlike firm, adherent ante-mortem thrombi with lines of Zahn, a gelatinous **postmortem clot** is soft, unattached to vascular walls, and separates into dependent dark currant-jelly erythrocyte portions and superior yellow chicken-fat serum layers.
steps.say: Postmortem clots are soft, unattached, and divide into currant-jelly and chicken-fat layers.

left.title: Ante-Mortem Thrombus
points: Dry, granular, and friable gross texture
Firmly adherent to underlying disrupted endothelial vessel wall
Exhibits distinct alternating microscopic lines of Zahn
Points of attachment leave an irregular, torn vascular intima

right.title: Post-Mortem Clot
points: Gelatinous, smooth, and moist gross surface
Completely unattached to the vascular wall, forming cast of lumen
Separates into dependent currant-jelly red and upper chicken-fat yellow zones
Lacks lines of Zahn and leaves completely smooth intact endothelium

steps.tx: The most prevalent inherited thrombophilia among individuals of Caucasian descent involves a single point mutation in coagulation factor V. In **factor V Leiden**, an arginine-to-glutamine substitution at position 506 abolishes the cleavage site for activated protein C, preventing factor V inactivation and promoting recurrent venous thromboembolism.
steps.say: Factor V Leiden resists cleavage by activated protein C, causing inherited hypercoagulability.

vis.alt: Inherited thrombophilia pathways and activated protein C resistance
vis.caption: Mechanisms of inherited thrombophilia and impaired endogenous anticoagulant pathways.

steps.tx: The second most common inherited cause of venous thrombosis involves a single nucleotide transition (G20210A) in the 3-prime untranslated region of the prothrombin gene. This inherited **prothrombin mutation** destabilizes mRNA degradation, yielding elevated circulating plasma prothrombin concentrations and an approximately threefold increased lifetime risk of deep venous thrombosis.
steps.say: The prothrombin G20210A mutation elevates circulating prothrombin levels, increasing thrombotic risk.

Enhanced mRNA Stability Elevates Prothrombin Biosynthesis

Threefold Elevated Risk of Recurrent Venous Thrombosis

steps.tx: Clinicians must recognize acquired hypercoagulable disorders driven by autoantibodies against plasma protein-phospholipid complexes. The **antiphospholipid syndrome** features anti-cardiolipin antibodies and lupus anticoagulant, paradoxically prolonging in vitro partial thromboplastin time while driving recurrent arterial and venous thrombosis and spontaneous pregnancy losses.
steps.say: Antiphospholipid syndrome causes recurrent thromboses and miscarriages despite prolonged in vitro PTT.

steps.tx: Hemodynamic differences dictate distinct morphological appearances between arterial and venous clots. Arteriolar thrombi typically initiate at sites of endothelial injury and plaque ulceration, consisting predominantly of platelet aggregates, whereas slow venous blood flow promotes fibrin meshwork trapping abundant erythrocytes, characterizing occlusive **arterial thrombosis** versus phlebothrombosis.
steps.say: Arterial thrombi are platelet-rich white clots, whereas venous thrombi are erythrocyte-rich red clots.

vis.alt: Arterial white thrombi versus venous red stasis thrombi
vis.caption: Pathological comparison of arterial platelet-rich thrombi and venous erythrocyte-rich thrombi.

steps.tx: If an established intravascular thrombus does not undergo early dissolution via endogenous tissue plasminogen activator fibrinolysis, capillary ingrowth and fibroblastic invasion occur. Over several weeks, endothelial-lined channels bore through the organizing fibrin mass, restoring partial luminal perfusion through the process of **thrombus recanalization**.
steps.say: Thrombus recanalization occurs as capillary ingrowth converts organized fibrin into new vascular channels.
